description: Broad examination of economic development, integrating both micro and macro perspectives. Explores factors that drive economic growth and influence development outcomes across countries. Students will analyze key challenges, evaluate development policies, and consider the role of empirical methods in assessing economic progress. By the end of the course, students will have a deeper understanding of the patterns of development and the policy approaches aimed at fostering economic growth and reducing global disparities. Prerequisite: ECON 500, ECON 501, ECON 502 and ECON 503, or consent of instructor.

subject: ECON
description: Introduction to financial economics and empirical finance, with the main focus being the study of core concepts in finance, comprehension of various finance models, and their application to real financial data. Begins with review essential background concepts, followed by an exploration of popular finance models. Students will engage in both analytical problem sets and data exercises as a way of reinforcing and understanding key lecture concepts. Prerequisite: FIN 500, ECON 502, and ECON 503 or consent of instructor. Restricted to students in the Policy Economics, MS program.

subject: ECON
description: Overview of different concepts, techniques, and algorithms in machine learning with a view towards applications in economics. Topics covered include regression, classification, model selection, predictive accuracy such as regularized regression, decision trees, boosting, support vector machines, and neural networks. Students acquire the skills to apply basic machine learning methods to solve economics problems. Prerequisite: ECON 500 and either ECON 502 or ECON 508.

subject: ECON
description: Provides a solid foundation in modern econometric methods for causal analysis, with a focus on their applications to policy-relevant questions. Covers a wide range of approaches for identifying causal relationships, including randomized controlled trials, observational studies, matching methods, difference-in-differences, synthetic control, regression discontinuity designs, instrumental variables, and local average treatment effects. Both theoretical underpinnings and practical application of each method are examined. By the semester’s end students will be critically equipped to assess, design, and evaluate causal inference strategies in applied economic research. Prerequisite: ECON 508 or both ECON 502 and ECON 503.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON 508 or both ECON 502 and ECON 503.

subject: ECON
description: Introduction to AI-assisted data analysis, with the focus being the study of core concepts in AI, machine learning and econometrics, and their application to structured and unstructured data with economic applications. Essential background concepts will be followed by an exploration of popular AI and ML models and how they are used in economics. Students will engage in both analytical problem sets and data exercises. Prerequisite: CS 225, CS 374, MATH 241, MATH 257, ECON 203, ECON 302 or their equivalents. Restricted to MS in Economics and Computer Science students, or with permissions of the instructor.

subject: ECON
course_name: Economics of AI and the Firm
description: Analysis of economics and management of artificial intelligence in organizations, with a focus on how firms can effectively adopt and implement AI technologies. Uses economic theory and empirics to understand how AI technologies influence productivity, pricing, organizational structure, labor markets, and competition. Applications are drawn from healthcare, retail, and finance sectors. Attention is given to empirical findings, theoretical models, and policy considerations related to automation, prediction, and algorithmic decision-making. Prerequisite: CS 225, CS 374, MATH 241, MATH 257, ECON 203, ECON 302 or their equivalents. Restricted to MS in Economics and Computer Science students, or with permissions of the instructor.

subject: ECON
description: The intersection of technology and society is examined, focusing on how human-computer interactions shape socioeconomic outcomes. Digital platforms, algorithms, and interfaces are analyzed for their impact on decision-making, labor markets, privacy, cultural consumption, and social equity. Frameworks are developed to evaluate technological changes, market dynamics, and policy responses. Students assess the societal implications of technical design and explore strategies for more equitable, sustainable digital futures. Prerequisite: CS 225, CS 374, MATH 241, MATH 257, ECON 203, ECON 302 or their equivalents. Restricted to MS in Economics and Computer Science students, or with permissions of the instructor.

subject: ECON
description: Introduces students to a variety of dynamic general equilibrium models that currently dominate the study of growth and economic fluctuations. These models include: neoclassical growth models, overlapping generations models, CAPM models, search models, and endogenous growth models. In covering these models, the course also seeks to develop a set of techniques for students to use. These techniques include discrete time optimization, continuous time optimization, dynamic programming and model calibration. Prerequisite: ECON 302 and ECON 303, or equivalent; calculus.

description: Development of modern macroeconomic theory, including disequilibrium theory, optimal short-term stabilization measures, and monetary, fiscal, incomes, and exchange rate policies; large-scale econometric models; linear and neoclassical growth models; aggregate distribution theory; money, capital movements, trade, and growth; optimal growth models; and exhaustible resources and growth. Prerequisite: ECON 531.

subject: ECON
description: The intersection of behavioral economics and technology is explored, integrating psychological insights into economic models for understanding digital-age behavior. Key concepts like default effects and heuristic thinking are covered, showing deviations from neoclassical rationality. Applications focus on tech industry and policy, examining market design and choice architecture including ethical considerations. Through lectures and projects, behavioral economics' role in shaping markets and policy is developed, including governmental applications of these insights. Prerequisite: CS 225, CS 374, MATH 241, MATH 257, ECON 203, ECON 302 or their equivalents. Restricted to MS in Economics and Computer Science students, or with permission from the instructor.

subject: ECON
description: The intersection of economics and computer science is explored, focusing on computational methods applied to strategic interaction problems. Game theory solutions for static and extensive-form games with complete and incomplete information are covered. Mechanism design is examined, exploring systems that incentivize desired behavior from self-interested agents through auctions, voting, and fair allocation. Algorithmic aspects including learning algorithms and computational complexity of finding equilibria are addressed. Applications in multi-agent learning, security, and electronic marketplaces are analyzed. Prerequisite: Restricted to MS in Economics and Computer Science students or consent of the instructor.

subject: ECON
description: The design of effective market mechanisms is explored, blending theoretical economic tools with computational approaches. Market analysis and engineering techniques are learned for improving resource allocation and efficiency in matching markets, auctions, and digital platforms. Practical applications are emphasized, drawing on real-world examples such as online advertising, school choice, and spectrum auctions, where case studies and empirical analyses are incorporated. Skills in both economic reasoning and algorithmic thinking are developed for designing and evaluating market mechanisms. Prerequisite: Restricted to MS in Economics and Computer Science students or with instructor permission.
